newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan guerrillas turn in last of weapons.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan guerrillas turn in last of weapons.

text.p: After 36 years of war, former guerrillas shouted triumph and sobbed goodbyes as they laid down the last of their weapons late on Friday in the Sacol disarmament camp in Guatemala's northern jungle.

More than 3,000 rebels have been living in eight different camps for three months, disarming under terms of a peace treaty signed on Dec. 29 between the government and the leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).

"This is the definitive end of the war. They can rejoin their loved ones and live as citizens with full rights and obligations," Raquel Zelaya, who heads a government-civilian commission to oversee compliance with the accords, said during a closing ceremony at Sacol camp.
The December treaty, which took five rocky years to negotiate, marked the end of one of Latin America's most drawn-out wars.
The guerrillas promised to give up their weapons in the peace accords. The army has pledged to cut its ranks by one third, give up its police role and to shut down several rural bases.
Right-wing business leaders and members of congress have questioned whether the URNG has turned in all its arms as many of the individual weapons turned in at the camps were old.
But U.N. observers said the URNG has also revealed caches of weapons and explosives that will be turned over.

A team of unarmed U.N. observers has overseen guerrilla disarmament in the different camps. The 200 ex-rebels who left Sacol, in the northern department of Peten, 250 miles (400 kms) from the capital, on Friday were the last to demobilize.

Under intense jungle heat, the men and women of Sacol, some carrying babies, lined up to receive demobilization certificates from the U.N. Among this group, the average had spent 15 years in clandestine jungle camps with the URNG.

"I began to fight with guerrilla in 1981. They (the army) killed my father and my brothers," said Samuel Contreras, who will lose his guerrilla name, Capt. Ronald. "We're content because our struggle has been worth the effort. Now we will become a political party."

Contreras and his comrades wept in each others' arms after they turned in M-16 and AK-47 rifles and prepared to get on buses that would take some to live with their families and others to temporary lodging for job training.
The government has promised land grants, education and aid for cooperative business projects for the ex-rebels.
